analysis.one_liner: Requires TV and internet providers to disclose full prices, itemize bills, and stop charging for customer-owned equipment.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill by voice vote on December 10, 2019, but the Senate committee it went to never voted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required cable, satellite, and internet providers to tell customers the full monthly price up front (including fees and when discounts expire), send an itemized electronic bill showing every charge separately, cancel a new contract without penalty within 24 hours of signing, and stop charging customers for routers or boxes the customer owns or never received. It also settled two behind-the-scenes fights: it made a satellite TV provision permanent for rural households, and it let small TV providers band together to negotiate against large broadcast companies that own many stations. The House passed it without a recorded vote; the Senate never took it up.
analysis.who_benefits: Households that pay for cable, satellite TV, or internet service. They would have gotten the true total price before signing a contract, an electronic bill that itemizes junk fees, taxes, and equipment charges separately, a 24-hour window to cancel a new contract without penalty, and the end of charges for routers and boxes the customer owns or never received. Rural households outside a TV station's local market would also have kept satellite access to distant broadcast signals.

how_it_helps.text: Providers must state the total monthly charge up front, explicitly noting promotional discounts and when they expire, plus every fee, before the customer signs [S5].
Electronic bills must itemize the service price separately from taxes, administrative fees, and equipment fees, and must show when the contract and any discount expire [S5].
Customers can cancel a new contract without early-termination fees during the 24 hours after the provider sends the contract copy [S5].
Providers may not charge for equipment the customer owns, equipment never provided, or equipment already returned (beyond the rental period) [S5].
The satellite retransmission provision for unserved households outside a station's local market, set to lapse at the end of 2019, was extended indefinitely [S3].
Small TV providers could designate a buying group to negotiate retransmission fees jointly against large broadcast station groups, adding countervailing power on the distributor side [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Cable, satellite, and internet providers, which would lose revenue from router rental fees and unitemized junk fees and would bear compliance costs. Large broadcast station groups would lose some of their negotiating leverage over retransmission fees, which are ultimately paid by subscribers.

drawbacks.text: The strongest protection was stripped in committee: the introduced version let customers cancel penalty-free when the total price increased mid-contract; the passed version kept only a 24-hour cancellation window after signing [S2, S3, S4].
The consumer rules apply only to services provided by cable and satellite distributors acting as such, so they would not cover customers whose internet provider is not also their TV distributor [S5].

The bill is a negotiated package: consumer protections were paired with retransmission provisions that relieve pressure on small distributors, so viewers get transparent bills while the underlying cost of broadcast fees is simply renegotiated, not capped [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are real but modest: the committee-amended version dropped the mid-contract price-increase exit, leaving only a one-day cancellation window and billing transparency. The bill would not have lowered the underlying fees themselves; it would mainly have made them visible and stopped equipment-fee overcharges. As passed, it was a lightweight version of what was introduced.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by voice vote under suspension of the rules on December 10, 2019, but the Senate Commerce Committee never voted it out, and it expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 12, 2019, and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee [S1, S7].
The subcommittee and full committee reported it as amended by voice vote on November 14 and November 20, 2019 [S7].
The House passed the amended bill by voice vote on December 10, 2019; no recorded roll call was taken [S4, S7].
The Senate received the bill on December 11, 2019 and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, which took no further action [S5, S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cable, satellite, and broadband providers kept unitemized junk fees and equipment rental charges, and large broadcast station groups kept their retransmission bargaining leverage, because the bill never became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: TV and internet providers and big broadcasters

for.name: Rep. Michael F. Doyle
for.role: House sponsor; moved to suspend the rules and pass the bill
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and moved the House to pass it as amended on December 10, 2019.

for.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill as amended by voice vote on December 9, 2019 (H. Rept. 116-329).

for.name: House of Representatives
for.what_they_did: Passed the bill under suspension of the rules, a fast-track procedure used for near-consensus bills, on December 10, 2019.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to in the Senate
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on December 11, 2019 and never voted it out before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No recorded votes exist: the committee reported it by voice vote and the House passed it by voice vote under suspension of the rules, and the bill had no cosponsors listed [S6, S7].

industries.note: They would lose equipment rental revenue and unitemized fee revenue to the billing rules, but they gain from the buying-group provision, which strengthens their hand against broadcasters in retransmission negotiations — savings that could lower subscriber bills. Their interest in the billing rules runs against viewers; their interest in retransmission reform runs alongside them [S3, S5].

The buying-group provision weakens their leverage to extract retransmission fees from small TV distributors; those fees are a line item on viewer bills. Their interest is in keeping the fee pressure, which conflicts with subscriber costs [S3].

industries.industry: Satellite TV subscribers and rural households outside local markets
industries.note: The direct-to-home retransmission authority they rely on was extended past its December 31, 2019 expiration [S3].
